notes.claim: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic as a perfect square plus a constant.
In letters, completing the square turns ax² + bx + c into a(x + b/2a)² + (c − b²/4a).
Writing a quadratic in completed-square form gives the coordinates of its turning point.
The MCA Second Engineer mathematics syllabus asks for stating and using the general formula for a quadratic; none of its lines read for this course names completing the square.
SQA's HN unit Engineering Mathematics 1 (H7K0 33) has no outcome on quadratics; it says it would be advantageous if learners had good algebraic skills on entry.

sources.title: Completing The Square | Brilliant Math & Science Wiki
sources.quote: Completing the square is a technique for manipulating a quadratic into a perfect square plus a constant. The most common use of completing the square is solving quadratic equations

sources.title: Completing the Square -- from Wolfram MathWorld
sources.quote: In modern notation, it converts a quadratic polynomial of the form ax^2+bx+c to the form * a(x+b/(2a))^2+(c-(b^2)/(4a)),

sources.title: The turning point and line of symmetry - Higher - Solving quadratic equations - Edexcel - GCSE Maths Revision - Edexcel - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: The coordinates of the turning point and the equation of the line of symmetry can be found by writing the quadratic expression in completed square form.
